description: Team of 5 from Guayaquil, Ecuador, tackling the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge. We're building an interactive browser to explore NASA's commercial Moon missions: landing sites, payloads and science, with a lunar map and timelines. We're CS engineering students skilled in React, Python, data and UI/UX. Looking for 1 more member with 3D/map visualization or video skills.
summary: Lunar Site Navigator compares lunar landing sites and dates in seconds. Using NASA LOLA terrain, LRO Diviner and Moon Trek data, it shows the Sun and Earth over each site's real horizon, how much solar power there will be, when there is direct line of sight to Earth, and where stable water ice is nearby — helping plan landings at the south pole.
details:
PROBLEM: The lunar south pole holds water ice in craters that never see sunlight, so NASA wants to land there. But the Sun barely rises above the horizon and terrain blocks it (nights up to 14 days in craters like Shackleton), and mountains can also hide Earth, cutting direct communication. Sunlight and line of sight change with every site and date, and a launch delay changes everything. Comparing sites today requires specialist tools (SPICE, GIS).

APPROACH: A browser-only web tool (JavaScript, canvas, WebGL/three.js; no server). Sun and Earth positions are computed with the open-source astronomy-engine library over each site's real horizon, built from LOLA terrain. Shadows are computed on the GPU; yearly Sun/Earth maps are precomputed with Node scripts included in the repository.

WHAT WE BUILT: (1) Site sky: panorama with LOLA terrain, Sun and Earth paths and countdowns. (2) South-pole map: light and shadow at a chosen instant plus yearly maps of % Sun, % Earth, stable ice and maximum temperature. (3) Site card: LROC orbital photo, slope and permanent shadow from Moon Trek, plus Diviner temperature and ice. (4) Side-by-side comparison of up to 4 catalog sites plus a custom south-pole point, with a score. (5) Launch-delay search for the next windows with Sun and Earth together. (6) A 3D Sun-Earth-Moon view.

RESULTS: Sun/Earth positions match JPL Horizons with a maximum error of 0.007 degrees over 1,428 comparisons. Our shadows agree 96.8% with LOLA's permanent-shadow mask. 97.7% of the surface ice flagged by Diviner lies where our independent map gives under 1% sunlight. Diviner temperatures differ from Apollo 15 and 17 in-situ measurements by at most 5.6 K (minimum) and 7.9 K (maximum).

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS: It is a quick pre-planning tool, not a replacement for SPICE-based mission analysis with high-resolution terrain; custom points work only at the south pole (latitude -90 to -80). Next: more sites and regions, higher-resolution terrain (LOLA 5 m, LROC) and plan export.
dataRefs: LRO / LOLA (LDEM_75S_240M, LDEM_16): terrain for each site's horizon, shadows, yearly light maps and slope.
LRO / Diviner (Polar Resource Product, Global Cumulative Product): surface temperature and water-ice stability.
NASA JPL Horizons: validation of Sun and Earth positions.
NASA Moon Trek (LROC NAC/WAC, LOLA slope, permanent shadow): site card and a catalog of 1,073 layers.
